composition: Nominal composition Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C (wt%), a high Mn–Al–C austenitic low-density steel. Mn (30 wt%) stabilizes the austenite; Al (11 wt%) and C (1.2 wt%) are the principal lightening/strengthening additions and together raise the stacking fault energy markedly (estimated SFE ~108 mJ/m² for the alloy). The Al and C contents also give high precipitation kinetics, leading to spinodal decomposition of nano-sized κ'-carbides in the austenitic matrix during quenching. The base element is Fe, and the microstructure remains essentially single-phase FCC austenite.
conclusions: Cold rolling of Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C austenitic low-density steel progressively refines the deformation substructure in the sequence Taylor lattice → microbands → twins → shear bands → dislocation tangles, a sequence distinct from tensile deformation. Strength rises strongly with reduction (ultimately ~2.0 GPa YS at 90%) while elongation falls. At the 50% reduction state, the deformation twins form at a resolved shear stress well below the calculated critical stress, attributed to short-range order and local stress concentration, and 50% is the reduction at which the rolling texture shifts from copper-type to brass-type, a transition ascribed jointly to dislocation planar glide and deformation twinning. The whole texture remains relatively weak because of planar glide. This work supplements prior tensile-deformation studies of high Mn–Al–C steels and, compared with earlier cold-rolling studies of e.g. Fe–30.5Mn–8.0Al–1.2C that were limited to 50% reduction and lacked TEM analysis, provides the full microscopic and textural evolution up to 90% reduction; it is relevant to lightweight automotive structural steels where cold-rolling processing and strength–ductility balance are critical.
mechanisms: Planar dislocation glide, a consequence of 'glide plane softening' in the high-SFE austenite, confines dislocations to single glide planes and produces the Taylor-lattice type low-energy dislocation structure (multiple approximately parallel slip bands) seen up to 50% reduction.

Because the interaction of non-coplanar slip bands at their intersections is not strong enough to completely impede glide, dislocations can cross the intersections and slip bands extend through whole grains; dislocation pile-ups nevertheless form at the band intersections.

Refinement of slip band spacing with increasing reduction (231 nm at 30% → 64 nm at 50%) provides strengthening through long-range interaction between coplanar slip bands (σTL = K·M·G·b/D), not dynamic Hall–Petch, in the low-reduction Taylor-lattice regime.

Microband boundaries form as geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) that accommodate the lattice misorientation between adjacent microband boundaries, giving the contrast difference between microbands and matrix.

Deformation twinning, normally prohibited at the alloy's high SFE, is activated at only ~0.75 GPa maximum resolved shear stress, far below the ~1.48 GPa critical shear stress calculated from τc = 2γSF/bp (γSF ≈ 108 mJ/m², bp = 0.146 nm); this is explained by (I) the actual critical shear stress being lowered by dislocation–short-range-order (SRO) interaction in the austenite, and (II) local stress concentration from inhomogeneous strain distribution.

The very fine twin–matrix (T-M) lamellae (~5.1 nm twins) restricted dislocations to the common {111} twinning/glide plane, causing abnormal rotation of matrix and twins toward higher Φ; as the twinning (glide) plane rotates nearly parallel to the rolling plane the resolved shear stress falls toward zero, so deformation can no longer be accommodated by glide and micro-shear bands nucleate from local strain concentration.

The weak overall rolling texture is attributed to dislocation planar glide, which causes unusual crystal lattice rotation and thereby weakens texture intensity (as in Ni-based L12 intermetallics where more difficult cross slip gives weaker texture); inhomogeneously deforming substructures (microbands, shear bands, twins) additionally scatter the texture.

The copper-type → brass-type texture transition at 50% reduction is attributed to two combined mechanisms: dislocation planar glide (as in Cu–Mn alloys) and deformation twinning (as in Cu–Zn and TWIP steels), the latter reflected indirectly by the development of the CuT component after 50% and the slight strengthening of the γ-fiber at 90%.

At higher reductions (50%–90%), microbands, nano-twins, shear bands and dislocation tangles/cells refine the structure and strengthen the steel through Hall–Petch-type effects, whereas at low reductions (10%–30%) strengthening is mainly slip-band spacing refinement; together these give the ultrahigh ~2.0 GPa yield strength at 90%.

The overall strength–ductility trade-off (increasing strength, decreasing elongation) is a direct consequence of this progressive substructural refinement and the accompanying loss of work-hardening capability.
microstructure: Characterized on the longitudinal section (RD × ND). After 50% cold rolling the single slip bands of the earlier stage are hardly distinguishable, but the material still retains a low-energy dislocation structure of Taylor-lattice type with refined slip band spacing (average 64 nm, reduced from 231 nm at 30%). Microbands cutting the matrix are formed with an average width of 166 nm (Fig. 5(a)); their different contrast relative to the matrix reflects a misorientation across their boundaries, which are geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) formed to accommodate that misorientation. In some grains, very fine parallel intermittent linear structures appear and are identified by selected-area diffraction (Fig. 5(c), foil normal [0 1 1]m, twin reflections indexed) and dark-field imaging (Fig. 5(d), imaged from the (–111)T reflection) as nano-scale deformation twins, with an average thickness of ~5.1 nm; the different diffraction contrast within a single twin indicates a high dislocation density inside the twin. The observed banded features lie oblique to the rolling direction (Fig. 3(c)). Overall the matrix phase remains FCC austenite. The rolling texture is weak. The {112}<111> Cu and {123}<111> S components increase up to 50% reduction and then decrease at higher strains; the copper-type to brass-type texture transition occurs at 50% rolling reduction, and a weak CuT ({552}<115>) component appears after 50%.
processing: The alloy was fabricated by vacuum induction melting, then soaked at 1250 °C for 12 h to homogenize and refine the cast microstructure, and hot forged into bars 60 mm in diameter with a finish forging temperature of 900 °C. Sheets of different thickness (1.3, 1.7, 2.4, 4 and 6 mm; 40 mm wide, 70 mm long) were cut from the bars by wire electrical discharge machining and solution treated at 1100 °C for 1 h before cold rolling. The present sample (proc_cr-50) is the sheet cold rolled to a 50% thickness reduction (equivalent strain ε = 0.1–2.3 series) after that 1100 °C/1 h solution treatment, i.e. cold rolling was applied to the as-quenched (austenite + κ'-carbide) material. This same processing pedigree (melting → homogenization → hot forging → solution treatment → cold rolling) is shared by all samples in the reduction series, of which 50% is the boundary case between the low-reduction (stage I) and high-reduction (stage II) regimes.
properties: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing (SHIMADZU AG-X 50KN universal testing machine, initial strain rate 10^-3 s^-1) was performed on dog-bone specimens cut along the rolling direction (gauge length 16 mm, width 4 mm), with three parallel tests per condition. Engineering and true stress–strain curves for the 50% reduction condition are plotted (Fig. 1(a) and (b)); no numeric YS/UTS/elongation values are labelled on the curves. The general trend of the reduction series is a progressive rise in yield strength accompanied by loss of work-hardening capability and decreasing uniform elongation; the as-quenched state had YS ~570 MPa, UTS ~830 MPa and uniform elongation exceeding 75%, while the highest (90%) reduction reaches ~2.0 GPa YS. In the true stress–strain curves the necking-point true stress is similar at low-to-medium reduction (<50%) and only rises sharply at higher reductions. No hardness, density, thermal, electrical, magnetic, corrosion or other physical/chemical property data are reported for this sample. Characterizations applied: optical microscopy (OM, electrolytically polished then etched in 1 g FeCl3 + 10 ml HCl + 10 ml deionized water), EBSD (TESCAN MIRA 3 SEM), TEM (JEOL 2100), and XRD texture measurement (Rigaku D/MAX 2500PC; incomplete {111}, {200}, {220} pole figures on the RD × TD plane, ODFs computed by the Arbitrarily Defined Cells method).
summary: This sample is a Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C (wt%) austenitic low-density steel cold rolled to a 50% thickness reduction, corresponding to the boundary between stage I (10%–50%) and stage II (70%–90%) reduction regimes of the paper's cold-rolling study. It is the intermediate-reduction state in which the deformation substructure changes markedly: single slip bands are hardly distinguishable, the Taylor-lattice type low-energy dislocation structure is refined (average slip band spacing 64 nm), and microbands (average width 166 nm) and nano-scale deformation twins (average thickness ~5.1 nm) coexist within some grains. Crystallographically it marks the reduction at which the rolling texture changes from "copper-type" to "brass-type".
unmapped: The 50% reduction condition is used as the reference state for Fig. 5 (TEM micrographs of microbands and nano-twins) and Fig. 3(c) (optical micrograph of the banded structure oblique to RD).

Characteristic SFE of the alloy is estimated as ~108 mJ/m² and the partial-dislocation Burgers vector bp as 0.146 nm, giving a calculated critical twinning shear stress of ~1.48 GPa versus a maximum resolved shear stress of ~0.75 GPa.
